extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers looking for a prescriptive story-structure template
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, page-targeted 15-beat story-structure template (Blake Snyder / Jessica Brody) adapted for novelists to map major turning points across a manuscript. Used to plan, diagnose, and pace a novel so each structural milestone occurs at a clear point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image (0-1%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A snapshot of the protagonist’s world before the story changes it — the “before” photo that establishes tone, setting, and the protagonist’s current state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: 0–1% of manuscript (approximate). Purpose: show the protagonist’s ordinary world so readers can later see change. Example: Katniss waking in District 12, showing poverty and protectiveness. Use this to establish mood/voice; it should clearly contrast with the Final Image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated (5%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone (usually not the protagonist) states the story’s thematic question or lesson; the protagonist doesn’t understand it yet but will by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: around 5%. Purpose: plant the thematic question or lesson early. Example: Gale’s comment in The Hunger Games that plants the seed of rebellion. Keep it brief and ideally voiced by a secondary character rather than spelled out by the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-Up (1-10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ~10% that establishes the protagonist’s world, flaws, relationships, and what needs to change; introduces main characters and shows what is missing in the protagonist’s life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: roughly 1–10%. Purpose: build the status quo and stakes so the Catalyst has meaning. Example: meeting Katniss’s family, her relationships, and distrust of the Capitol. This section should make clear what the protagonist stands to lose or gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst (10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inciting incident — the single event that knocks the protagonist’s world off its axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~10%. Purpose: a clear, unmistakable event that propels the story forward. Example: Prim’s name called at the reaping. Note: “This beat should be unmistakable. If a reader cannot point to your Catalyst, it is not strong enough.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate (10-20%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist reacts to the Catalyst — questioning, resisting, preparing, or debating what to do; the ‘should I go?’ phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: roughly 10–20%. Purpose: show internal conflict about whether to accept the journey/choice presented by the Catalyst. Example: Katniss volunteering, saying goodbye, and grappling with the Games. Use this to clarify stakes and the protagonist’s reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Two (20%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist makes a choice that propels them into Act 2 — leaving the old world and entering the new (crossing the threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~20%. Purpose: an active choice that moves the story into the central conflict rather than remaining in setup or reaction. Example: Katniss arriving at the Capitol and entering the reality of the Games.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story (22%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new character or relationship enters, usually carrying the story’s theme — often a love interest, mentor, ally, or foil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: around 22%. Purpose: provide thematic resonance and emotional growth that informs the protagonist’s arc. Example: Peeta as a representation of a different survival ethic. The B Story frequently supplies the insight that resolves Act 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games (20-50%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘promise of the premise’ — the section where the book delivers what the premise promises (e.g., attending a wizard school, investigations and chases in a thriller).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: roughly 20–50%. Purpose: deliver the scenes readers expect and explore the central concept. Example: training, interviews, sponsor strategy, and early arena moments in The Hunger Games. This is where the core genre elements and set-piece sequences live.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint (50%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A midpoint reversal that raises the stakes — either a false victory (things seem great but will collapse) or a false defeat (things seem terrible but a new path opens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~50%. Purpose: pivot the story and escalate stakes or understanding. Example: the rule change allowing two victors, which alters Katniss’s strategy. Use the Midpoint to shift goals or deepen commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In (50-75%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal and external pressure intensifies: enemies regroup, allies falter, and the protagonist’s flaws resurface; what was gained at the Midpoint begins to erode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: roughly 50–75%. Purpose: create mounting obstacles and complications that test the protagonist. Example: the Careers hunting Katniss and Peeta, Rue’s death, eroding trust and increasing danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost (75%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest point — a death (literal or metaphorical) or irretrievable loss that creates the story’s dark night of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~75%. Purpose: deliver a gut-punch that makes victory seem impossible and forces reflection. Example: the rule change revocation that threatens what Katniss fought for. This beat should feel final and devastating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul (75-80%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The emotional aftermath of All Is Lost — the protagonist sits in despair, grief, or hopelessness; the ‘whiff of death’ that makes the finale meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~75–80%. Purpose: allow the protagonist to emotionally process the loss and reach a turning realization. Example: Katniss confronting the possibility of killing Peeta or dying herself. Use this to set up the insight that leads to Break into Three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Three (80%)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new plan emerges — often sparked by the B Story — where the protagonist synthesizes lessons learned and chooses a final course of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~80%. Purpose: provide the protagonist’s active decision and strategy for the Finale. Example: Katniss deciding to defy the Capitol and use the nightlock berries as leverage. This beat converts theme and B Story insight into action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale (80-99%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist executes the plan, confronts the antagonist using lessons learned in Act 2, and ties up converging story threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~80–99%. Purpose: resolve conflicts through the protagonist’s growth; deliver the climax and consequences. Example: Katniss and Peeta’s joint suicide threat forcing the Capitol’s hand. Ensure actions reflect the arc and thematic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image (99-100%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘after’ photo that mirrors the Opening Image and shows how the protagonist has changed; the distance between Opening and Final Images is the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: ~99–100%. Purpose: give readers a clear sense of transformation and consequence. Example: Katniss returning to District 12 as a changed person and symbol of rebellion. Use contrast with Opening Image to underline growth or loss.
